title: Views and Templates
description: Learn how Razor views generate dynamic HTML in ASP.NET Core MVC. Covers Razor syntax, layouts, partial views, view imports, and how to pass data from controllers to views.

blocks.text: **Views** are the pieces of your application that users actually see in their browsers. They take data from the controller and turn it into HTML. In ASP.NET Core, views use **Razor syntax** — a combination of HTML markup and embedded C# code — to generate dynamic content.
Understanding views is essential because they are where the user experience happens. Well-structured views are clean, readable, and easy to modify without touching controller logic.
Razor Syntax Basics

Razor view files have the `.cshtml` extension and live in the `Views/` folder. Razor lets you switch between HTML and C# fluidly using the `@` symbol. When Razor sees `@`, it treats everything after it as C# code until the context returns to HTML.

blocks.title: Common Razor syntax patterns
items: `@Model.PropertyName` — Output a property value from the model
`@foreach (var item in Model.Items) { ... }` — Loop over a collection
`` — Tag Helper that renders a model property

blocks.text: Strongly Typed Views

At the top of a Razor view, the `@model` directive declares the type of data the view expects. This is called a **strongly typed view** — it means the compiler knows what properties are available on the model, giving you IntelliSense and compile-time error checking.

blocks.content: A Razor view that receives a Product model and displays its properties as HTML.

blocks.text: In this view, `@Model` accesses the `Product` object passed from the controller. The `@if` block conditionally renders a badge based on the price. Tag Helpers like `asp-action` and `asp-controller` generate correct URLs automatically.
Views for Collections
Many views display a list of items. Razor handles this naturally with `@foreach`, iterating over the model collection and rendering HTML for each item.

blocks.content: Use @foreach to loop over a collection of products and render each as an HTML list item.

blocks.text: Layouts: Shared Page Structure

Most websites have a consistent layout — a header, navigation bar, footer, and possibly a sidebar — that appears on every page. Rather than repeating this HTML in every view, ASP.NET Core uses **layouts**. A layout is a shared template that wraps around individual views.

The default layout file is `Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml`. Each view specifies its layout at the top with `Layout = "_Layout"`. Inside the layout, `@RenderBody()` marks where the individual view's content appears.

blocks.title: _ViewStart.cshtml
blocks.text: The `_ViewStart.cshtml` file runs before every view in its folder (and subfolders). It is the standard place to set `Layout = "_Layout"` so you do not have to repeat it in every view.
Partial Views

**Partial views** are reusable chunks of HTML that you can embed inside other views. They are perfect for UI elements that appear on multiple pages, such as product cards, comment sections, or navigation menus.

blocks.text: View Imports and View Start

Two special Razor files reduce boilerplate across all your views: `_ViewImports.cshtml` and `_ViewStart.cshtml`. They live in the `Views/` folder and apply to every view in that folder and its subfolders.

blocks.title: What each file does
items: **_ViewImports.cshtml** — Imports namespaces and adds tag helpers so you don't need `@using` or `@addTagHelper` in every view
**_ViewStart.cshtml** — Sets the default layout for all views so you don't repeat `Layout = ...` in every file
Both files are optional but strongly recommended for reducing repetition

blocks.text: Passing Data: ViewData, ViewBag, and Strongly Typed Models
There are three common ways to pass data from a controller to a view. Each has tradeoffs in type safety, readability, and convenience.

blocks.title: Data passing options
items: **Strongly typed model** — Pass a typed object to `View(model)`. The view declares `@model Product` for full IntelliSense and compile-time safety. Recommended for most cases.
**ViewData** — A dictionary (`ViewData["Key"] = value`). Values are stored as `object` and require casting. Useful for one-off values like page titles.
**ViewBag** — A dynamic wrapper around `ViewData`. Write `ViewBag.Message = "hi"` without casting. Convenient but no compile-time checking.

blocks.title: Prefer strongly typed models
blocks.text: Strongly typed models are the most robust option. They catch errors at compile time, provide IntelliSense, and make views self-documenting. Use ViewData or ViewBag only for small, simple values that do not justify a dedicated model.

terms.definition: A markup syntax for embedding C# code into HTML files. Razor views (.cshtml) are the default way to generate dynamic HTML in ASP.NET Core MVC.
A shared template (_Layout.cshtml) that wraps around individual views, providing consistent header, navigation, and footer across all pages.
A reusable view fragment that can be embedded inside another view. Used for components like cards, forms, or navigation elements that appear on multiple pages.
A view that declares its model type with @model, enabling compile-time type checking and IntelliSense for model properties.
Server-side attributes (e.g., asp-for, asp-action) that generate HTML. Tag Helpers provide an HTML-friendly alternative to HTML Helper methods.

blocks.description: Build a view that renders a list of products as HTML cards using Razor syntax, a partial view, and a layout.
steps: In the Views/Products folder, create `Index.cshtml` with `@model IEnumerable<MyFirstApp.Models.Product>`

Add a `

Product Catalog

` heading and a `
    ` element
Use `@foreach` to loop through the products and render each as a list item with the product name and price
Create a partial view `_ProductCard.cshtml` in Views/Products that renders a single product's name, price, and a Details link
Replace the `<li>` content with `<partial name="_ProductCard" model="product" />`

blocks.expectedOutcome: The `/Products` page renders a list of products, each displayed as a card with the name, formatted price, and a Details link. The page uses the shared layout and the product card partial view.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Razor views (.cshtml) combine HTML markup with C# code using the @ symbol
The @model directive makes a view strongly typed for compile-time safety and IntelliSense
Layouts provide consistent page structure across all views via _Layout.cshtml
Partial views let you reuse UI components like product cards across multiple pages
_ViewImports.cshtml and _ViewStart.cshtml reduce boilerplate across all views
Prefer strongly typed models over ViewData/ViewBag for passing data to views
blocks.takeaway: Views are the user-facing layer of your application. Mastering Razor syntax, layouts, and partial views lets you build clean, maintainable user interfaces that are easy to update as your application grows.
